## THE CURRENT MAP
7:9/q01 What does the balance or weighing at Judgment signify? [مَوَٰزِينُهُۥ · theology] (turns on: Whether the balance is a physical instrument, a figure for justice, or a measure of truth in acts; whether deeds have bodily weight and what the weighing demonstrates.)
  7:9/q01/p1 A real balance is set up and publicly weighs on Judgment Day. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya cites the visible balance in a Prophetic report and warns against abandoning the apparent sense; Ibn al-Jawzi cites hadith. The majority describe a beam, two pans and tongue. Ibn Kathir cites 21:47 and other judgment verses; al-Tabataba'i reports large-pan narratives but treats their form as explanatory imagery.
  7:9/q01/p2 The balance is a figure for exact justice, judgment, or the abundance of good deeds. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya quotes Abu Talib's poetry, then rejects this reading. Razi cites figurative Arabic weights, 18:105 and a poem on equal arguments; he argues deeds are accidents and literal weighing adds no knowledge. Imam al-Sadiq likewise says attributes lack bodily weight and God needs no weighing. Study Quran links commercial and cosmic balance verses.
  7:9/q01/p3 Deeds are tested against the truth proper to each act; that truth is their measure. — reasons: Al-Tabataba'i says prayer, almsgiving, speech and other acts have distinct standards; the book makes their truth manifest (39:69; 45:29). He rejects arbitrary balances and argues justice needs a criterion for mixed deeds; prophets and successors embody right action and belief.
  7:9/q01/p4 The scale can be read inwardly as justice, with sense and intellect as its pans. — reasons: Qashani distinguishes enduring rational virtues, sincere intentions and good works from transient sensations, desires and vices; the former bear weight at a lesser resurrection.
  7:9/q01/p5 Reason, knowledge and sound will act as moral balances. — reasons: Al-Tha'labi reports reason distinguishing truth and falsehood, knowledge distinguishing lawful and unlawful, and sound will distinguishing felicity and misery.
7:9/q02 Why is mawāzīn plural? [مَوَٰزِينُهُۥ · grammar] (turns on: Whether grammatical plurality points to Arabic usage, weighed things, components, separate instruments, or separate measures of truth.)
  7:9/q02/p1 The plural may denote a single balance by Arabic usage. — reasons: Al-Tha'labi and al-Baghawi compare other Arabic plurals; al-A'sha's line has plural breasts and forearms for one each, and al-Baghawi cites 'messengers.' Al-Zajjaj offers this too, but Razi objects that the plain plural permits several scales.
  7:9/q02/p2 The plural reflects the many deeds or records weighed on one balance. — reasons: Al-Zajjaj and the majority reported by Abu Hayyan use the plurality of weighed things; al-Tabataba'i objects that this does not establish the criterion for mixed deeds.
  7:9/q02/p3 There are multiple balances or standards, perhaps for persons or kinds of acts. — reasons: Razi prefers several balances from the plain plural and 21:47, possibly for acts of heart, body and speech. Al-Tabataba'i assigns distinct truths to prayer, almsgiving, fasting and pilgrimage.
  7:9/q02/p4 Each servant has a separate balance. — reasons: Al-Baghawi reports the view and Abu Hayyan attributes it to Hasan; Ibn Atiyya rejects Hasan's account, distinguishing one balance from each person's individual weighing.
  7:9/q02/p5 One great balance has a separate balance suspended for each servant. — reasons: Al-Tha'labi reports this alternative; al-Baghawi states it separately from a simple individual balance.
  7:9/q02/p6 The plural names the balance's combined parts. — reasons: Al-Tha'labi and al-Baghawi list two pans, beam and tongue or indicator, all needed for weighing.
7:9/q03 What is weighed? [مَوَٰزِينُهُۥ · referent] (turns on: Which object or quality receives weight, and whether multiple reported objects can all be weighed.)
  7:9/q03/p1 Written records of deeds are weighed. — reasons: Al-Tha'labi and Ibn Atiyya reason that deeds are accidents and weight belongs to bodies. The ninety-nine scrolls and testimony card report illustrates this; Ibn Kathir says al-Tirmidhi graded it sound. Abu Hayyan says God creates weight in the records. Bursevi reports this as the majority view.
  7:9/q03/p2 Deeds themselves are weighed, made bodily or appearing in forms. — reasons: Ibn Abbas describes believers' deeds as beautiful and unbelievers' as ugly; Ibn Kathir cites traditions of the Qur'an, suras and righteous deeds appearing in forms. Al-Tabataba'i distinguishes moral qualities from physical movements, yet allows embodied appearance.
  7:9/q03/p3 The persons themselves may be weighed. — reasons: A heavy glutton weighs less than a gnat's wing; Ibn Kathir also cites Ibn Masud's thin legs outweighing Uhud and 18:105. Bursevi repeats the huge man's report.
  7:9/q03/p4 Only the ending of a person's deeds is weighed. — reasons: Wahb ibn Munabbih says God grants good or evil endings according to what He wills for the servant.
  7:9/q03/p5 The truth contained in each deed is weighed. — reasons: Al-Tabataba'i says one standard measures each act; true worship has weight and false acts none. The book discloses this truth (39:69; 45:29), and prophets and successors can embody its standard.
  7:9/q03/p6 Deeds, their records or forms, and their doers may all be weighed at different times. — reasons: Ibn Kathir reconciles the deed-form, scroll-card and person-weight reports rather than forcing one object.
  7:9/q03/p7 Lasting rational virtues, intentions and deeds carry weight, not passing sensations. — reasons: Qashani's inward account places intellect and sense in the pans and distinguishes lasting from transient qualities.
  7:9/q03/p8 Only deeds undertaken for God's pleasure and reward in the hereafter have weight. — reasons: Islahi cites 18:103–105: acts without those aims count as evil and lack weight.
7:9/q04 What makes the scales heavy or light? [خَفَّتْ مَوَٰزِينُهُۥ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether weight expresses net good versus evil, the presence of good or truth, inward quality, divine acceptance, or physical heaviness.)
  7:9/q04/p1 Good deeds make them heavy, while few or absent good deeds leave them light. — reasons: Mujahid explains light scales as scant good works; Ibn Ashur calls lightness a matching metaphor for their absence. Hasan says the good-deed pan should grow heavy while sin's pan grows light. Ali ibn Abi Talib's report says good deeds add weight and sins lighten it.
  7:9/q04/p2 Good and bad deeds are compared; whichever exceeds the other determines the result. — reasons: Razi divides people by predominance and denies equal totals; Jabir and Ibn Abbas report one deed or grain can tip the result. Study Quran attributes the light balance to evil outweighing good.
  7:9/q04/p3 Truth, sincerity and right intention give a deed weight; falsehood has none. — reasons: Al-Tabataba'i uses prayer, almsgiving and speech as examples of distinct truths. Abu Bakr and al-Harith contrast following truth with falsehood; Islahi makes seeking God's pleasure and the hereafter decisive. Qashani weighs sincere lasting virtues.
  7:9/q04/p4 A person's inner reality outweighing their outward state gives a heavy balance; the reverse gives a light one. — reasons: Ali's report gives this criterion; al-Tabataba'i transmits it but says it is not an explanation of these verses.
  7:9/q04/p5 God's pleasure can make even a single date of charity fill the scale. — reasons: David asks how the vast balance can be filled; God gives this answer in the reports of Ibn al-Jawzi and Bursevi.
  7:9/q04/p6 Heaviness is downward tendency inherent in a heavy object, or its composing parts; lightness is absence of heaviness. — reasons: Jishumi reports Abu Hashim's distinct-attribute account and Abu Ali's parts account, noting their agreement about lightness.
7:9/q05 Who are those whose scales are light? [وَمَنْ خَفَّتْ مَوَٰزِينُهُۥ · referent] (turns on: Whether the wording restricts the light-scaled to deniers or includes sinful believers, and what counts as weighty good.)
  7:9/q05/p1 They are disbelievers who deny God's signs. — reasons: Muqatil's identification is repeated by al-Wahidi; Razi reports it as the majority view because 'wronging Our signs' means denial. Al-Nasafi says without faith no good works count. Al-Baghawi and others connect their lightness with denial.
  7:9/q05/p2 They include anyone whose evil deeds exceed the good, including sinful believers. — reasons: Razi gives the two unequal totals; Abu Hayyan says the apparent division includes obedient and sinful believers and unbelievers. Ibn Abbas and Jabir give a one-deed tipping rule; Study Quran reports the predominance of evil.
  7:9/q05/p3 They have no good deeds with weight or deeds lacking the required truth. — reasons: Ibn Ashur calls lightness the absence of good deeds; al-Tabataba'i says false works have no truth-weight. Islahi says acts not aimed at God's pleasure or the afterlife carry no weight.
7:9/q06 Are unbelievers' deeds weighed? [مَوَٰزِينُهُۥ · theology] (turns on: Whether unbelievers' works can carry weighable merit or whether 18:105 and 25:23 rule out their weighing.)
  7:9/q06/p1 Yes; the apparent division includes unbelievers, and some of their deeds can be weighed. — reasons: Abu Hayyan includes believers and unbelievers; al-Qurtubi, as reported by Alusi, says deeds not dependent on Islam can lessen punishment, citing Abu Talib. Ibn Abbas's report gives unbelievers' deeds an ugly light form.
  7:9/q06/p2 No; the balance and records are for Muslims, while unbelievers' deeds have no weight. — reasons: Others cite 25:23 or 18:105. The Najmi interpretation says only people of truth and their deeds are weighed; Ali ibn al-Husayn says polytheists go in groups to Hell. Al-Sakhawi treats Abu Talib's mitigation as exceptional.
  7:9/q06/p3 Unbelievers lack faith and thus lack good works counted in the scale. — reasons: Al-Nasafi uses this t

<<7:9 update 1, part 1 of 0..2>>
o explain their light balances; Ibn Ashur describes polytheists as devoid of good in this passage.
7:9/q07 Can the scales balance equally, and where do mixed or sinful believers fit? [خَفَّتْ مَوَٰزِينُهُۥ · theology] (turns on: Whether equal totals exist, whether the binary address includes mixed believers, and whether success means immediate or eventual deliverance.)
  7:9/q07/p1 The two outcomes exhaust people; no one has equal good and bad totals. — reasons: Razi explicitly denies an equal group. Ibn Ashur says the passage's purpose addresses believers with good and polytheists devoid of it, leaving mixed believers aside.
  7:9/q07/p2 Equal deeds place a person among the people of the Heights. — reasons: Ibn Abbas says a single deed or grain can change the outcome; Alusi reports identifying the omitted equal group with those in 7:46.
  7:9/q07/p3 The passage leaves mixed believers outside its immediate purpose. — reasons: Ibn Ashur says they are treated elsewhere; Alusi reports a reply putting them among people with mixed deeds in 9:102 and notes God's promised fulfillment.
  7:9/q07/p4 Sinful believers may first have deeds weighed without tawhid, then tawhid tips the balance when they leave Hell. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya reports this answer twice to the question how a successful heavy-scaled sinner can enter Hell; the testimony of divine oneness is added after an initial weighing.
  7:9/q07/p5 A sinful believer's eventual release from Hell itself counts as success despite earlier discipline. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya gives this answer twice; the question arose because heavy scales and temporary Hell seemed in tension.
  7:9/q07/p6 Faith's testimony can rescue a believer whose good deeds appear light. — reasons: Al-Wahidi attributes this to Ibn Abbas and reports a prayer card. Razi contrasts prayer card and testimony card, and reports al-Qadi's qualification that testimony must be joined to its duties. Ibn Atiyya says testimony of divine oneness must tip a person's balance.
7:9/q08 What is the purpose of weighing if God already knows? [مَوَٰزِينُهُۥ · theology] (turns on: How a visible weighing relates to God's knowledge, justice, public proof, and the criterion of judgment.)
  7:9/q08/p1 It makes judgment and justice visible, establishes proof, and ends excuses. — reasons: Al-Tha'labi compares a truthful record (45:29); Ibn Atiyya likens recording and limb testimony; Ibn al-Jawzi says it displays fate and deeds. Abu Hayyan cites questioning, admission, limbs, prophets and angels. Study Quran links 7:6 and says the scale reassures people; Z says it rebukes wrongdoers. Razi reports increased joy or shame. Ibn al-Jawzi says God reports deeds to messengers and nations despite already knowing them; Ibn Abbas says the placed record speaks of the deeds.
  7:9/q08/p2 It tests faith during life and distinguishes the saved from the doomed hereafter. — reasons: Al-Tha'labi and Ibn al-Jawzi state both purposes; the public caller reports lasting felicity or misery.
  7:9/q08/p3 The measure reveals how much truth each deed contains and assigns proportional recompense. — reasons: Al-Tabataba'i says the placed book identifies each deed's truth (39:69; 45:29); without a criterion mixed deeds would be judged arbitrarily.
  7:9/q08/p4 Weighing is unnecessary as a physical way for God to discover deeds. — reasons: Razi argues deeds cannot physically be weighed and a display adds no information; Imam al-Sadiq says God knows every amount already. Al-Tabataba'i clarifies this denies worldly physical weight, while embodied deeds and manifest justice remain possible.
7:9/q09 What do the reported scales and attendants look like? [مَوَٰزِينُهُۥ · reports] (turns on: The reported form, scale, location and agents of the Judgment balance; Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan question detailed shape reports.)
  7:9/q09/p1 A balance has a tongue or pointer and two pans. — reasons: Ibn Abbas, Hasan and the majority describe the instrument. Ibn Atiyya says reports of more precise dimensions and shape are unreliable.
  7:9/q09/p2 Gabriel oversees the scale and settles wrongs between people. — reasons: Hudhayfa says victims receive the oppressor's good deeds; if none remain their sins transfer to him. Ibn Atiyya calls Gabriel custodian.
  7:9/q09/p3 One vast scale faces the Throne, with pans toward Paradise and Hell, large enough for the heavens and earth. — reasons: Ibn Salam gives the location, size and Gabriel's presence; Aisha's report likens the pans to heaven and earth, with a swordlike path; Salman transmits a similar account. Al-Tabataba'i treats such imagery as accessibility for simple hearers.
  7:9/q09/p4 A caller or angel announces lasting bliss or misery when each balance is weighed. — reasons: Ubayd Allah ibn al-Ghayzar sets it amid the crowded Resurrection; Ibn al-Iyzar places the caller beside the scale; Anas has an angel announce the result.
7:9/q10 What does the card that outweighs ninety-nine records bear? [مَوَٰزِينُهُۥ · reports] (turns on: Which words the rescuing card bears in the distinct reports.)
  7:9/q10/p1 It bears the testimony that there is no deity but God and Muhammad is His messenger. — reasons: Ibn Umar and Abd Allah ibn Amr transmit ninety-nine vast sin scrolls against a tiny card; Ibn al-Jawzi names Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi, and Ibn Kathir reports al-Tirmidhi graded it sound. Bursevi explains a card as a price tag sewn to clothing.
  7:9/q10/p2 It bears the believer's blessings upon the Prophet, who produces and identifies the card. — reasons: Al-Wahidi gives this further report with a fingertip-sized card; Razi contrasts it with the more widespread testimony-card account.
7:9/q11 When do people fail to remember one another at Resurrection? [مَوَٰزِينُهُۥ · reports] (turns on: Which stages of the Resurrection reports include; the accounts can describe more than one stage.)
  7:9/q11/p1 At the balance, until each learns whether it is heavy or light. — reasons: Aisha's report says people are barefoot and unclothed and occupied with records and weighing, citing 80:37; Qatada's report also names the balance.
  7:9/q11/p2 When records fly, until each sees where the book lands. — reasons: Aisha's continuation cites 69:19; Qatada's report also names this stage.
  7:9/q11/p3 At the bridge over Hell, while hooks and thorns detain people. — reasons: Aisha's continuation and Qatada's report name the bridge.
7:9/q12 What do light scales lead to? [خَفَّتْ مَوَٰزِينُهُۥ خَسِرُوٓا۟ أَنفُسَهُم · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the result is described as eternal punishment, a deed-total outcome, or wasted human capacity.)
  7:9/q12/p1 They lead to ruin, Hell, and lasting misery. — reasons: Ibn Abbas gives an unbeliever's ugly deeds and Fire; Ibn Atiyya says the good-deed pan rises and the lost remain eternally in Hell; al-Tabrisi and al-Wahidi identify punishment. Callers announce lasting wretchedness.
  7:9/q12/p2 They register punishment according to the excess of bad over good. — reasons: Jabir and Ibn Abbas state the prevailing side determines Paradise or Hell; one deed can tip it.
  7:9/q12/p3 They show a person has wasted the capacity and sound nature that could have brought benefit. — reasons: Al-Baydawi and Alusi speak of original disposition, while Qashani describes exchanging capacity for worldly debris and ego aims.
7:9/q13 What does it mean to lose themselves? [خَسِرُوٓا۟ أَنفُسَهُم · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the loss stresses destroyed capital or disposition, punishment, or the lost Paradise home.)
  7:9/q13/p1 The self is one's chief capital, lost like a merchant's investment. — reasons: Jishumi, al-Haddadi and al-Biqa'i use the capital image. Ibn Ashur explains loss as the opposite of profit and cites 6:20 and 2:16.
  7:9/q13/p2 They destroy their own selves or capacity for benefit through punishment and bad action. — reasons: Ibn Abbas says arriving at punishment; Ibn Atiyya and al-Tabrisi describe destruction and eternal Hell. Baydawi and Alusi say they waste innate disposition; Qashani says worldly aims replace original capacity.
  7:9/q13/p3 They lose their home in Paradise as well as themselves. — reasons: Ibn Abbas's report names both losses.
7:9/q14 What are 'Our signs' here? [بِـَٔايَٰتِنَا · referent] (turns on: How broadly the signs are identified, and whether the Imam report gives a general sense or one example.)
  7:9/q14/p1 They are God's proofs, indications, commands and prohibitions. — reasons: Tabari calls them proofs requiring affirmation; Ibn Atiyya adds commands and prohibitions, and Nasafi calls them proofs.
  7:9/q14/p2 They include what Muhammad brought from God. — reasons: Muqatil identifies denial of the Qur'an's divine origin; Ibn Abbas via al-Wahidi and al-Tabrisi name Muhammad's message.
  7:9/q14/p3 Denial of the Imams is a concrete instance of wronging the signs. — reasons: Al-Tabataba'i reports this interpretation but explicitly treats it as one instance within the wider sense.
7:9/q15 What does 'wronging Our signs' mean? [بِـَٔايَٰتِنَا يَظْلِمُونَ · meaning] (turns on: Whether injustice is glossed as denial, broader refusal to give signs their due, or a reported specific instance.)
  7:9/q15/p1 It means denying or disbelieving the signs, suppressing their evidence and refusing to follow them. — reasons: Ibn Qutayba notes the several senses of zulm; Tabari says rejecting proofs despite their validity. Ibn Ashur says denial suppresses established truth; Bursevi calls it placing denial where belief belongs.
  7:9/q15/p2 It means persistently putting the signs in the wrong place or failing to give them their due. — reasons: Al-Biqa'i and Elmalili emphasize continued misplacement; Ibn Ashur reads the imperfect as repeated past denial. Qashani takes ego display and concealing divine qualities as this injustice.
  7:9/q15/p3 It can include denying the Imams as a particular case. — reasons: Al-Tabataba'i says a report supplies this instance of a broader meaning.
7:9/q16 How do the preposit

ions and mā in the final clause work? [بِمَا كَانُوا۟ بِـَٔايَٰتِنَا يَظْلِمُونَ · grammar] (turns on: How the two bi- phrases attach, whether mā is nominal, and what sense licenses bi- after 'wronging'.)
  7:9/q16/p1 Bi-mā gives the cause of loss, with mā as a verbal noun. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya likens the causal bi- to thanking someone for what they did. Al-Samin attaches the phrase to 'lost'; Bursevi and Alusi agree. Ibn Ashur links it to persistent wrongdoing.
  7:9/q16/p2 Bi-āyātinā attaches to 'wronging' because the verb includes the sense of denying or rejecting. — reasons: Abu Hayyan, al-Samin and Bursevi explain the nonusual construction by implied denial; al-Samin compares 3:11 and 27:14. Islahi says the implication also includes wronging oneself.
  7:9/q16/p3 The construction compresses denial of revelation and self-wronging into one expression. — reasons: Islahi calls it tadmīn and says the suppression conveys a comprehensive meaning briefly.
7:9/q17 Why is 'Our signs' placed before the verb, and what does the tense convey? [بِـَٔايَٰتِنَا يَظْلِمُونَ · rhetoric] (turns on: Whether the order serves cadence, emphasis, or both; how the verbs depict duration.)
  7:9/q17/p1 The prepositional phrase is advanced for the verse ending. — reasons: Al-Samin and Alusi point to the rhyme or end cadence.
  7:9/q17/p2 Fronting the signs gives them emphasis. — reasons: Ibn Ashur says the placement highlights the signs.
  7:9/q17/p3 Past kānū with imperfect yaẓlimūn depicts repeated, persistent past wrongdoing. — reasons: Alusi and Ibn Ashur both read ongoing denial in the combined verb forms.
7:9/q18 Why does a singular 'whoever' take the plural 'those'? [وَمَنْ فَأُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ · grammar]
  7:9/q18/p1 Man is singular in form but plural in sense, so the result uses a plural; a singular result would also be eloquent. — reasons: Tabari explicitly gives both grammatical possibilities.
7:9/q19 How does this outcome connect to the surrounding passage? [* · links] (turns on: Whether the link emphasizes sequence, guidance, or parallel language of justice and records.)
  7:9/q19/p1 The heavy and light clauses explain the result of the earlier weighing after questioning and accounting. — reasons: Razi places weighing after earlier questioning; Ibn Ashur identifies the conditionals as its outcomes. Ibn Kathir cites other heavy/light judgment passages including 21:47, 23:102–103 and 101:6–11.
  7:9/q19/p2 The opening verses urge following guidance and warn of the cost of rejecting it. — reasons: Study Quran describes verses 1–10 this way; the named wrong against signs supplies the warning here.
  7:9/q19/p3 The balance image is linked to just balances elsewhere and to a truthful record. — reasons: Al-Tha'labi cites 21:47 and 45:29; al-Tabataba'i invokes 21:47, 39:69 and 45:29. Study Quran joins judgment balance with fair commercial measures and cosmic balance passages.
7:9/q20 What does weighing mean in ordinary language? [مَوَٰزِينُهُۥ · meaning]
  7:9/q20/p1 It compares things to disclose relative measure and extends figuratively to patterned verse and measured speech. — reasons: Jishumi gives the lexical extension; al-Farra reports mizan used for equality or proximity and cites a poem of a person's words. Razi cites a poetic argument-measure.
7:9/q21 How do judgment and mercy affect the measured result? [مَوَٰزِينُهُۥ · theology]
  7:9/q21/p1 God rewards or punishes by deed quantity and quality while mercy, repentance and intercession may increase reward or forgive. — reasons: Kuranyolu cites 6:160: good can be rewarded more than its equivalent and evil receives equivalent punishment; these allowances do not violate justice. Ibn Kathir stresses God wrongs no one (4:40).

## THE NEW NOTES
[DAMGHANI:v1p309/r6] DAMGHANI, d. 478 · author | holds | To wrong God’s signs means to deny the Qur’an, Torah, or signs by rejecting that they come from God.
[JISHUMI:v4p2504/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Questioning, weighing, reckoning, and testimony would have no purpose if God could punish people without first establishing their case.
